resumen: How to use roads, tracks and corridors to lead the eye to your subject.

bloques.alt: Two drawings of a straight road that narrows in the distance, with a person far away, over a rule-of-thirds grid. On the left, the vanishing point is in the center of the photo: 1, center, suits symmetrical scenes. On the right, the vanishing point is on a crossing of the grid, at a third: 2, on a third, more dynamic than in the center.
bloques.pie: 1 Vanishing point in the center: suits symmetrical scenes. 2 On a third: more dynamic than in the center.

bloques.texto: Lines that meet in the distance lead the eye: put the subject where they end, or place the vanishing point on purpose.

[[lineas-guia|Leading lines]] lead the eye through the photo to the subject. When lines are parallel in real life (a road, train tracks, a corridor), in the photo they seem to meet at a [[punto-de-fuga|vanishing point]] and give a sense of depth.

items: Roads, tracks, paths, bridges, fences, rivers and rows of trees.
Better if they start in the foreground: that way they run through the whole photo.
Diagonals run from the foreground to the background and add depth.

bloques.texto: Where to put the vanishing point

In the center it suits symmetrical scenes, like a corridor or a straight road. On a crossing of the rule-of-thirds grid it is usually more dynamic. If you put the subject on the vanishing point or in front of it, the lines work like arrows pointing at it.

items: Get close to where the lines begin and lower the camera: they converge more.
A wide angle makes the lines longer and exaggerates the perspective.
If you move a few steps or change the height, the lines join the foreground and the background differently.

bloques.texto: Turn on the grid to put the vanishing point on a crossing. On many phones, 0.5x is a wide angle: it lengthens the lines and exaggerates the perspective.
Lines that meet toward the horizon add depth. The verticals of a building that meet because you tilted the camera usually look like a mistake: see “Architecture photography”.

Find a road, a path or a corridor. Take a photo with the vanishing point in the center and another moving until it sits on a third. If you can, put someone far away and see how the lines point at them.
